summary.summary: Portsmouth ended the year with gross debt of £718m (including £56m of PFI) against investments of £230m — net debt £488m — and took no new borrowing at all, running £292m of internal borrowing instead while new money costs over 5%. Its borrowing need (CFR) is £1,010m, so £292m of real borrowing is deferred, not avoided; the council itself notes this needs ongoing monitoring as the need grows. Net treasury costs came in £0.01m under budget.

news_drafts.headline: Portsmouth forecasts £1.052m schools grant overspend, with High Needs £524k over budget
news_drafts.lead:
Portsmouth's schools budget is forecast to overspend by £1.052m in 2026-27, according to first-quarter figures for the Schools Forum. The dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) started the year with a carried-forward deficit of £8.014m. Its high needs block, which pays for children with special educational needs and disabilities, is forecast at £40.797m against a £40.273m budget, an overspend of £524k.

The paper attributes this to more pupils than budgeted. There are 30 more full-time-equivalent pupils than the 1,086 budgeted with education, health and care plans (legal documents setting out a child's support) in mainstream schools (£356k), 32 more at The Harbour School (£262k) and 68 more post-16 pupils at City of Portsmouth College (£173k). Placements with other local authorities are costing over 50% more than budgeted (£122k), and opening an inclusion centre adds £51k. A £546k underspend on the Early Years Inclusion Fund partly offsets this, because a planned centre is not opening and pupil numbers are lower than forecast.

Separately, the Department for Education cut early years funding by £1.0m in July after the January 2026 census. As in previous years, the council offset the cut against the carried-forward deficit, which reduced the balance available for high needs pressures. That raised the budgeted overspend from £537k to £1,525,200. The papers give a high needs funding shortfall of £7.527m and say the grant is ring-fenced, so its deficit cannot be offset against the council's general fund.
news_drafts.paper_title: Dedicated Schools Grant 2026/27 (Quarter 1) Budget Monitorig and Revised Budget

news_drafts.headline: Portsmouth's temporary accommodation rose to 551 households in Q1 2026/27 from 459 a year earlier, driving £3.2m overspend
news_drafts.lead: Portsmouth's financial pressures are shifting from temporary budget gaps to structural demand growth that existing reserves cannot sustain. Temporary accommodation demand rose to 551 households in the first quarter of 2026/27, up from 459 a year earlier, driving a £3.2m overspend—the single largest pressure on the budget. Adult social care costs rose by £1.3m and children's placements by £0.86m, all driven by rising client volumes and placement costs. The council covered £7.5m of gross portfolio overspends by releasing £3.8m from contingency reserves and transferring £3m from earmarked reserves, leaving just £0.66m reported deficit. However, the deputy chief executive warned that "demand for services continues to place pressure...there remains longer term uncertainty relating to further increases in demand," signalling that budget pressures are unlikely to ease without structural change.

news_drafts.headline: Portsmouth faces three-year audit backlog and may not clear accounts until 2028
news_drafts.lead: Portsmouth's auditors have warned that the council will not achieve a fully unqualified audit opinion until after 2027/28, leaving its financial accounts lacking full independent verification for a third consecutive year. The external auditor, EY, issued a qualified opinion for 2024/25 because prior-year disclaimers had prevented sufficient audit evidence being gathered over major assets and reserves. During last year's audit, EY discovered a £30m error in how properties were valued in 2023/24, now flagged as a significant risk. Before rebuilding assurance can begin, the council must complete a comprehensive reconciliation of reserves across all disclaimed years. The timeline for recovery extends beyond the current financial year because properties are revalued on a five-year rolling programme, with the next full cycle not completing until 2027/28. EY says it may not move beyond a qualified opinion until after that date.

findings.paper_title: Dedicated Schools Grant 2026/27 (Quarter 1) Budget Monitorig and Revised Budget
findings.headline: Average cost of SEND placements in other local authority schools increased by over 50% against budget with no change in pupil numbers
findings.detail: The number of Portsmouth pupils placed in other local authority schools remained consistent with budget, but average costs per place have increased by over 50% compared to February 2026 budget assumptions, creating a £122k overspend. This suggests significant cost inflation in inter-council placements, possibly reflecting competitive pressure between councils for SEND provision.
findings.matters: Budget setting methodology may be weak or cost escalation is outpacing past trends; indicates inter-council placement costs are escalating faster than anticipated; suggests Portsmouth is competing with other councils at higher rates.
findings.figures: Average placement costs up 50%+ against budget; resulting overspend £122k (Element 3 Top Up - OLA School: budget £515.5k, forecast £637.1k, variance £121.6k)
findings.quote: the number of Portsmouth pupils being placed in other local authority schools has not changed, however the average costs of those places have increased by over 50% than budgeted, resulting in a forecast overspend of £0.122m.

findings.paper_title: Dedicated Schools Grant 2026/27 (Quarter 1) Budget Monitorig and Revised Budget
findings.headline: Early Years DSG funding reduced by £1.0m following January 2026 census, offset against carry forward and increasing overall DSG budgeted overspend
findings.detail: DfE adjusted Early Years funding in July 2026 based on census data from September 2025 to March 2026, resulting in £1.0m reduction. Following council practice, this was offset against DSG carry forward rather than managed within Early Years services, reducing the balance available to offset High Needs pressures and increasing the DSG budgeted overspend from £537k to £1.525m.
findings.matters: Demonstrates external funding volatility; the council's practice of offsetting census adjustments against carry forward reduces flexibility to manage other pressures; indicates pupil numbers lower than forecast.
findings.figures: Early Years funding reduction £1.0m; DSG budgeted overspend increases to £1,525k (from £537k); impact on carry forward balance (£1.012m)
findings.quote: The Early Years Block adjustment in July 2026 resulted in a reduction in funding of £1.0m following the January 2026 census for the period September 2025 to March 2026. As in previous years the reduction has been offset against the DSG carry forward, which has reduced the balance available to offset the High Needs pressures. Thus, increasing the DSG budgeted overspend to £1,525,200.

findings.paper_title: Dedicated Schools Grant 2026/27 (Quarter 1) Budget Monitorig and Revised Budget
findings.headline: DSG forecast to carry forward deficit of £1.052m into 2027-28, constrained by High Needs funding shortfall of £7.527m that cannot be fully offset by contingencies
findings.detail: Portsmouth entered 2026-27 with a carried-forward deficit of £8.014m. Q1 shows expenditure exceeding income by £537k, with year-end forecast overspend of £1.052m. The council has committed growth fund (£461m potential carry forward), contingency (£124k), and relational practice reserves (£124k) to offset the High Needs shortfall, but the DSG is ring-fenced so deficits cannot be offset against general fund.
findings.matters: A growing carried-forward DSG deficit constrains schools' budgets in following years; ring-fencing means this cannot be resolved from general fund; signals structural mismatch between DSG funding levels and service demand, typical of post-COVID EHCP surge across English councils.
findings.figures: Forecast carry forward deficit £1.052m; High Needs funding shortfall £7.527m; starting carry forward deficit (£8.014m); schools contingency and growth fund £585k total; carry forward balance brought forward 2025-26 (8,014)
findings.quote: Overall, the budget is forecast to overspend by £1.052m, the details of which are set out in the sections below.

findings.paper_title: Dedicated Schools Grant 2026/27 (Quarter 1) Budget Monitorig and Revised Budget
findings.headline: High Needs block forecast to overspend by £524k, driven by 30 additional mainstream EHCP pupils, 32 additional special school pupils, and placement costs 50% higher than budgeted
findings.detail: The overspend comprises EHCP mainstream £356k (30 FTE pupils above the budgeted 1,086), special schools £262k (32 pupils above budget at The Harbour School), inclusion centre opening £51k, post-16 £173k (68 pupils above budget at City of Portsmouth College), and other local authority placements £122k (costs increased over 50% against budget). Partially offset by an Early Years Inclusion Fund underspend of £546k where a planned centre is not opening and pupil numbers are lower than forecast.
findings.matters: EHCP demand and inter-council placement costs are both exceeding budget assumption, signalling structural cost pressures; if trends continue, 2027-28 overspend will be larger. High Needs funding is chronically underfunded across English councils.
findings.figures: High Needs overspend £524k (budget £40,273k, forecast £40,797k); EHCP mainstream 30 FTE above 1,086 budgeted (+£356k); special schools 32 pupils above budget (+£262k); post-16 68 pupils above budget (+£173k); other LA placements costs up 50%+ (+£122k); Early Years Inclusion Fund underspend £546k
findings.quote: The High Needs block is forecast to overspend by £0.524m per Table 2 and the following paragraphs set out the reasons for the forecast position.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget Monitoring 2026/2027 (First Quarter) to end June 2026
findings.headline: Treasury management underspend of £747,700 from higher interest rates, but council flags budget as volatile and rate-dependent.
findings.detail: The council has benefited from 'sustained higher interest rates' providing increased returns on short-term cash holdings. However, the paper explicitly notes the Treasury budget is 'potentially a very volatile budget particularly in the current economic climate and is extremely susceptible to both changes in interest rates.' This is clearly flagged as a one-off benefit.
findings.matters: Shows the council is not in complete freefall (interest rates are helping), but this benefit is temporary. If rates fall, this income disappears and the underlying £7.5m overspend becomes fully visible.
findings.quote: The forecast underspend is largely because of the sustained higher interest rates which has provided the Council with increased levels of interest on its short-term cash flows.
